transcript.text: Bosch SMS25AW00G, came back to E:09 on the display and the dishes are washed but stone cold. Is this an expensive fix?

The error code E:09 (or sometimes just 09) on Bosch dishwashers typically indicates a water temperature issue. Specifically, it means the water did not reach the required temperature during the wash cycle. This explains why your dishes are washed but "stone cold"—the machine detected that the heating element wasn't functioning correctly or the water wasn't hot enough, so it may have stopped early or completed the cycle without proper sanitization/heating.

### Is this an expensive fix?
Generally, no—it is usually a moderate-cost repair. Here’s why:

#### 1. Most Common Cause: Faulty Heating Element
• The heating element is a wear-and-tear part that can fail over time.
• Cost: A replacement heating element for a Bosch SMS25AW00G typically costs €30–€60 (or $40–$80 USD) if you buy the part yourself.
• Labor: If you hire a technician, labor charges will add €50–€100+ depending on your location and whether it’s an emergency call-out.

#### 2. Other Possible Causes (Less Common but Cheaper)
• Thermostat or Temperature Sensor Failure: These are smaller parts and may cost less than the heating element itself.
• Loose Wiring or Connection: Sometimes a simple reconnect fixes the issue. This is very cheap if caught early.
• Control Board Issue: Rare, but possible. If the main PCB is faulty, this could be more expensive (€100–€200+ for the part).

### Steps to Diagnose & Fix:
1. Reset the Dishwasher:
• Turn off the power at the circuit breaker or unplug it for 5–10 minutes.
• Restart and run a short cycle. If the error persists, it’s likely hardware.

2. Check the Heating Element:
• Look inside the bottom of the tub for visible damage to the heating element (burns, breaks).
• You can test it with a multimeter for continuity (resistance should be ~20–40 ohms). If it’s open circuit (infinite resistance), the element is dead.

3. Call a Professional?
• If you’re not comfortable working with electrical components, hire a technician. Ask them to diagnose first before committing to a full repair. A simple heating element replacement shouldn’t exceed €150–€200 total (parts + labor) in most regions.

### Bottom Line:
• DIY Fix: ~€30–60 for the part.
• Professional Repair: ~€150–250 total, depending on location and technician rates.
• Not a catastrophic failure—this is one of the more common and affordable repairs for Bosch dishwashers.

If your dishwasher is under warranty, contact Bosch support immediately—this repair may be covered free of charge.
Thanks. I'm in the UK so prices in pounds please. I've got a multimeter and could check the heater, but is it safe to do that, and how would I go about it?

Yes, it is generally safe to test the heating element with a multimeter, provided you follow strict safety precautions. The key rule is: never test electrical components while they are live (connected to power).

### ⚠️ Critical Safety Steps Before You Begin:
1. Turn off the mains power to the dishwasher at the circuit breaker or fuse box. Do not rely on just switching it off at the control panel.
2. Unplug the dishwasher if possible, or ensure the isolation switch is off.
3. Wait 5–10 minutes after disconnecting power. Capacitors in the control board can hold a charge; waiting ensures they discharge.
4. Double-check with your multimeter that there’s no voltage present at the heating element terminals before touching them.

---

### How to Test the Heating Element:

#### Step 1: Access the Heating Element
• Remove the bottom rack and any lower spray arm if necessary.
• The heating element is usually a U-shaped or coiled metal tube at the bottom of the tub.
• You may need to remove a few screws (often Torx T20) holding it in place, but you don’t necessarily need to fully disconnect it from the wiring harness unless it’s very tight.

#### Step 2: Set Your Multimeter
• Turn your multimeter to Ohms (Ω) setting. Use the lowest range that can measure up to ~100 ohms (e.g., 200 Ω).

#### Step 3: Test for Continuity
• Touch one probe to each of the two terminals on the heating element (the metal prongs where it connects to the wiring).
• Good Reading: You should get a resistance reading between 20–40 ohms. This indicates the heating element is intact and functional.
• Bad Reading: If you see “OL” (Open Loop), “1” on the display, or an extremely high number (like 999+), the heating element is broken internally and needs replacement.

#### Step 4: Check for Earth Fault (Optional but Recommended)
• Set your multimeter to continuity mode (beep setting).
• Touch one probe to a metal terminal on the heating element and the other to the metal body of the dishwasher tub.
• Good Reading: No beep / infinite resistance. This means there’s no short to earth.
• Bad Reading: If it beeps or shows low resistance, the heating element is leaking current to the casing—this is a serious fault and the element must be replaced immediately.

---

### If the Heating Element Is Faulty:
#### Cost in the UK:
• Part Only: £30–£50 (e.g., from parts4appliances.co.uk, bosch-home.com, or Amazon).
• Labor: If you call a technician, expect to pay £80–£150 for labor + VAT.

#### DIY Replacement:
• It’s straightforward: unscrew the old element, disconnect the wires (take a photo first!), connect the new one in the same way, and screw it back in.
• Ensure the rubber gasket/seal around the element is intact to prevent leaks.

---

### If the Heating Element Tests Fine:
If your multimeter shows 20–40 ohms and no earth fault, the issue may be elsewhere:
1. Thermostat/Temperature Sensor: Can fail and send false readings. Test for continuity (should be near 0 ohms when cold, changing slightly with heat).
2. Control Board: Less common, but possible. If both heating element and sensor are good, the board may not be sending power to the heater.

### Recommendation:
Start by testing the heating element as described. It’s the most likely culprit for E:09 + cold dishes. If it fails, replace it yourself or hire a local engineer. If it passes, consider calling a professional to check the thermostat and control board, as further DIY diagnosis can be tricky without schematics.
